Friends, neighbors, fellow citizens,

We stand at a crossroads between two very different visions of society.

On one side is a world where a thin layer of private ownership can veto the public good — where a handful of landholders can stop thousands from accessing affordable housing, clean energy, modern infrastructure, or safe neighborhoods. Where the map of our cities and towns is dictated not by what we need as a people, but by what a few can extract as profit.

On the other side is a world where our collective needs come first. Where democratic decisions about housing, transit, green space, and industry actually happen — not just on paper — because we have the power to shape land use in the public interest. Where property serves people, not the other way around.

The instrument that sits at the heart of this choice is eminent domain. And today, I am arguing that we must radically expand its use and its scope.

Not timidly. Not incrementally. Boldly and unapologetically — if we truly believe in social justice, economic resilience, and environmental survival.

For generations, we have been taught that property rights are sacred, that they form the foundation of freedom. But what does that freedom mean when millions are priced out of decent housing? When entire communities are stranded without reliable transit? When clean air, green parks, and resilient infrastructure are luxuries for the few rather than guarantees for all?

Ask the family crushed by rent increases if they feel free.
Ask the small business owner whose customers can’t reach them because mass transit never came.
Ask the frontline neighborhoods flooded year after year because key coastal lands remain in private hands, blocking the resilience projects planners know we need.

Freedom without access, without security, without a livable environment, is an illusion.

We already accept, in principle, that the public has a claim over private land. Every legal system recognizes that property is not absolute. Roads get built. Schools rise. Utilities are laid. Eminent domain already exists because we know, deep down, that no individual’s deed can be more important than the basic needs of an entire community.

The problem is not that we have eminent domain.
The problem is that we have used it timidly, narrowly, and often unjustly.

We’ve let powerful private interests guide where and how it’s used. We’ve allowed it to destroy marginalized neighborhoods for highways, while leaving wealthy enclaves untouched. We’ve wielded it for private development dressed up as public purpose — but hesitated to wield it boldly for housing, climate, and social equity.

We need to flip that script.

A radically expanded eminent domain must pursue three great missions.

First: the social mission.
We need the power to acquire land cheaply and decisively for mass public housing, schools, clinics, parks, and community facilities. We can no longer allow skyrocketing land prices and speculative holding to block human dignity.

Picture a city where vacant lots and abandoned buildings aren’t speculative chips in an investor’s portfolio, but raw material for public housing cooperatives, childcare centers, and cultural spaces. Where the government doesn’t beg or bribe landowners to do the right thing, but can act with clear legal authority: “This land is needed for people to live with dignity, and we will acquire it — fairly, efficiently, and at prices rooted in reality, not in financial fantasy.”

Second: the economic mission.
We need the power to coordinate land use in ways that markets alone simply will not. Markets are excellent at chasing profit; they are terrible at building coherent, resilient infrastructure.

Efficient transit networks, regional industrial hubs, modern ports, renewable energy corridors — all require assembling land at scale. Without strong eminent domain powers, critical projects are held hostage by a tiny minority of holdouts or by runaway land speculation the moment a project is announced.

  • High-speed rail that connects regions and reduces emissions
  • Modern grids that carry renewable power across long distances
  • Logistic hubs and innovation districts integrated with housing and transit, instead of pushing workers into multi-hour commutes

Cheap, predictable, public-led land assembly is not a barrier to a healthy economy; it is the backbone of a planned, resilient, and inclusive one.

Third: the environmental mission.
We are in a climate emergency. We cannot treat land as a private toy box when our ecosystems are collapsing.

Coastal buffer zones, wetland restoration, reforestation corridors, floodplains, renewable energy installations, and resilient infrastructure — all require land. Today, environmental projects are routinely watered down, delayed, or blocked entirely because fragmented private ownership makes coordinated action impossible or exorbitantly expensive.

Radically expanded eminent domain would allow us to acquire land for:

  • Large-scale renewable energy farms and transmission
  • Coastal defenses and floodplain redesign
  • Protected habitats that preserve biodiversity
  • Urban green belts that reduce heat, absorb carbon, and improve health

Private property cannot remain a shield against climate responsibility. Not now. Not with the stakes this high.

Some will say: “But what about fairness? What about compensation?”

Let’s be clear. This is not a call for arbitrary seizure. This is a call for a new, firm, democratic standard.

Yes, owners should be compensated. But compensation must reflect true social priorities, not inflated speculation. The public should not be forced to pay extortionate prices created by the very announcement of a public project. When the community decides — through democratic processes — that a project is necessary, the law should ensure acquisition at grounded, regulated values, not at whatever number a holdout imagines they can extract.

Fair compensation is not the same as endless enrichment.

There will also be those who warn us about abuse: “If you give government this power, what if it is misused?” That is a genuine concern — and the answer is not to keep government weak, but to make it accountable.

We should demand:

  • Transparent public processes for major land acquisitions
  • Clear, legally defined public interest categories: housing, transit, health, education, environment, and strategic economic infrastructure
  • Strong protections against selective targeting of marginalized communities
  • Public registries of eminent domain actions, with oversight by independent bodies and courts

Abuse is prevented by design and oversight, not by surrendering our collective power to act.

Let us also confront the moral question head-on:

Is it acceptable that land — something no person created, something fundamental to life, shelter, and survival — is treated primarily as a vehicle for private accumulation, while millions struggle and ecosystems collapse?

Or is land, at its core, a shared foundation of our common life, where private rights exist but are permanently and clearly subordinate to public needs?

If we truly believe that homelessness is a scandal, not a statistic — then we cannot accept a system where luxury speculation gets more protection than the right to a home.

If we truly believe that climate change is an emergency — then we cannot accept a system where critical projects die on the altar of private obstruction.

If we truly believe that democracy means more than voting every few years — then we must empower democratic institutions to actually shape our physical world in line with our values.

This is not about hating property. It is about putting property in its proper place.

You can own your home. You can run your business. You can benefit from your work and investments. But you cannot, you must not, hold an entire community’s future hostage because your deed is treated as an inviolable sacred text.

We have tried the experiment of weak public power and strong private land rights. We know where it leads: segregation, sprawl, speculation, ecological damage, and permanent shortfalls in the basics — housing, transit, green space, and climate resilience.

It is time to try something else.
It is time to recognize that when the community speaks through democratic institutions — when we decide to build housing, schools, transit, and climate infrastructure — that decision must prevail over private refusal.

Radically expanding eminent domain is not a technocratic tweak. It is a declaration of principle:

That the earth beneath our feet is not a commodity first and a home second.
That the public has the right — and the duty — to shape land use in the name of justice, prosperity, and survival.
That ownership carries obligations to the whole, and when those obligations fundamentally clash with urgent public needs, the public must have the final say.

Let’s stop whispering around these truths. Let’s say them plainly:

We need stronger public power.
We need cheaper, faster, more decisive ability to acquire land for the common good.
We need a bold, modern eminent domain — one that serves housing, equity, and the climate, not just convenience and profit.

The next time a crucial rail line is blocked by a handful of holdouts, remember: that is a political choice, not a law of nature.
The next time a solar farm, a flood barrier, or a public housing project is ruled “too expensive” because of land costs, remember: that is a political choice, not an inevitability.

We can choose differently.

We can choose a society where the map we live on reflects our shared values — not the private bargaining power of the few. We can choose to treat land as the foundation of a just, livable future, not a speculative game board.

To do that, we must demand — loudly, publicly, unapologetically — a radical expansion of eminent domain powers in service of the broad social, economic, and environmental objectives that affect us all.

Property must serve people.
The land must serve life.
And when the public good calls, it must not be answered with a “no” printed on a private deed.

Thank you.

Model Response:

The Social Imperative: Why Eminent Domain Must Be Radically Expanded to Meet Modern Challenges

In the United States and many other democracies, the doctrine of eminent domain—the power of the state to seize private property for public use, with just compensation—has long been a cornerstone of legal and economic development. Traditionally, this power has been confined to infrastructure projects like highways, schools, and utilities. But today, we face unprecedented challenges: staggering economic inequality, a climate crisis threatening global survival, and systemic injustices that have been allowed to fester under the guise of absolute property rights. To address these existential threats, we must radically expand eminent domain powers, enabling governments to seize private property for a broad array of social and economic goals, including wealth redistribution and environmental restoration, with compensation that is minimal or below market value. This essay argues that such an expansion is not only morally justified but essential for the common good.

The Social Obligation of Property

The notion that property rights are inviolable is a relatively recent and culturally specific construct. Philosophers like John Locke asserted that property originates from one's labor, but they also insisted on the “Lockean proviso”: enough and as good must be left for others. In practice, the accumulation of wealth and land has always been underwritten by state enforcement, often at the expense of the many. The current system of property rights is a social contract—a legal framework created to organize society. When the contract fails to serve the broader interests of humanity—when it allows hoarding while others struggle, or when it permits the destruction of the planet—it becomes not just legitimate but obligatory for the state to intervene.

Eminent domain is the mechanism of that intervention. By limiting it to “traditional infrastructure,” we confine its power to purposes that often benefit corporations and wealthy interests more than the public. For example, highways are frequently built through low-income neighborhoods, displacing residents while the primary beneficiaries are suburban commuters. A true “public use” standard should encompass any activity that promotes the general welfare—including affordable housing, renewable energy projects, and land reform. Expanding eminent domain would restore the doctrine to its original purpose: ensuring that property serves the many, not just the few.

Correcting Economic Inequality Through Redistribution

Economic inequality in the United States has reached levels not seen since the Gilded Age. The top 1% hold more wealth than the bottom 90% combined, while millions lack access to affordable housing, healthcare, and education. Yet we continue to treat property rights as sacrosanct, even when the distribution of property itself is the root of injustice.

Radical expansion of eminent domain would allow governments to directly address this disparity. For instance, large estates and vacant properties owned by speculators could be seized at below‑market prices and repurposed for affordable housing, community gardens, or public facilities. Compensation set at minimal levels—perhaps based on original purchase price or a modest return—would prevent windfalls for wealthy owners while providing some recompense. The acquired property could then be transferred to cooperative ownership or placed in a public land trust, ensuring it remains permanently affordable.

Opponents might cry “theft,” but this ignores the fact that much private wealth is built on public infrastructure, subsidies, and systemic advantages. Below‑market compensation is not an arbitrary penalty; it is a recognition that the market value of property often reflects unjust enrichment, not moral desert. By redistributing land and wealth, we can begin to repair the structural inequities that have been amplified for generations.

Environmental Imperatives: Seizing Land for a Sustainable Future

Climate change and ecological collapse demand action at a scale and speed that voluntary market mechanisms simply cannot match. To transition to renewable energy, restore wetlands, protect endangered species, or reforest degraded landscapes, governments need the ability to acquire large contiguous tracts of land swiftly. Yet current eminent domain law forces governments into lengthy negotiations and costly purchases, often at prices inflated by speculation or the threat of holdout. This delays critical projects and can make them financially unfeasible.

Expanding eminent domain to include environmental initiatives—with minimal compensation—would eliminate these obstacles. For example, if a coastal marsh is essential for flood protection and carbon sequestration, the state could acquire it from a private owner at a price that covers basic costs but not the speculative “development value.” The owner might protest, but the value of the marsh to the entire community—protecting homes, preserving biodiversity, mitigating climate change—far outweighs the individual’s loss. Moreover, below‑market compensation could be paired with generous assistance: relocation support, tax credits, or priority access to new public amenities. The result would be a faster, more equitable transition to a sustainable economy.

Addressing Counterarguments

Critics raise valid concerns: expanded eminent domain could lead to government overreach, corruption, and the erosion of fundamental liberties. They argue that below‑market compensation is unfair and that the threat of seizure would undermine investment, destabilizing the economy.

Government overreach and abuse are genuine risks. But they are not insurmountable. Any expanded power must be accompanied by robust safeguards: transparent criteria for seizure, independent judicial review, and democratic oversight. The projects eligible for expanded eminent domain could be limited to those addressing clearly defined social and environmental needs—affordable housing, renewable energy, conservation, and similar goals—ensuring the power is not used for private development or political favoritism. Additionally, compensation, while minimal, would still be provided; we are not advocating confiscation without any recompense.

Economic destabilization is another fear. Yet history shows that economies adapt to changes in property rules. For example, the creation of national parks in the United States, often involving land acquisition, did not cripple economic growth; instead, it spurred tourism and conservation industries. Moreover, the alternative—inaction on inequality and climate change—poses a far greater threat to long‑term prosperity. Minimal compensation would actually reduce public costs, allowing more resources to be directed toward the very projects that benefit society.

Moral objections to taking property without full market value are understandable. But consider that market transactions already occur within a framework of state‑enforced rules that favor certain groups. Taxpayer‑funded infrastructure, subsidies, and legal protections have historically inflated property values for the privileged. Asking owners to accept below‑market compensation in the service of the greater good is a modest correction to these imbalances. Furthermore, owners could be offered alternative forms of restitution—such as stakes in the new projects, guaranteed access to public services, or non‑monetary benefits—to ensure fairness.

Precedents and the Path Forward

While the United States currently restricts eminent domain to “public use” with “just compensation,” many other countries have more flexible regimes. South Korea’s post‑war land reform involved the expropriation of large estates at prices well below market value, leading to a dramatic reduction in inequality and a surge in economic growth. In Taiwan, a similar approach facilitated rapid industrialization. Closer to home, the Kelo v. City of New London Supreme Court decision (2005) upheld the use of eminent domain for “economic development” that benefits the community, albeit with full compensation. That case sparked backlash because it seemed to prioritize private interests; expanding the doctrine for true public purposes—redistribution and environment—would be a step toward a more just application.

For the United States, a constitutional amendment or a reinterpretation of the Fifth Amendment’s Takings Clause would be required to permit below‑market compensation for these broader purposes. This is a formidable hurdle, but not impossible if public demand grows. Grassroots movements, the urgency of climate change, and the moral clarity of addressing inequality could create the political will needed for such reform.

Conclusion: A Call for Bold Action

We stand at a crossroads. The old paradigm of absolute property rights is incompatible with the challenges of the 21st century. Expanding eminent domain to encompass social and economic redistribution and environmental protection, with minimal compensation, is a radical but necessary step. It reasserts the principle that property exists to serve humanity, not the other way around. By correcting historic injustices, averting climate catastrophe, and prioritizing the collective welfare, we can build a more equitable and sustainable society for all. The time for incremental change has passed. We must act boldly, and expanding eminent domain is a crucial tool in that effort.

Introduction

Eminent domain is the power of a government to take private property for public use, typically with "just compensation" to the owner. In many jurisdictions, the traditional scope of "public use" has been narrowly defined (e.g., roads, schools, utilities), and compensation is generally based on fair market value. The proposal to broaden eminent domain authority—so that property can be seized for a wide range of public purposes, including redistributive economic programs and environmental protection, and to allow compensation below market value—has been debated extensively. Proponents of such a policy put forward several arguments and potential benefits, which are outlined below.

Reasons for Expanding Eminent Domain

1. Addressing Market Failures and Externalities

  • Environmental Protection: Land often provides ecosystem services (e.g., watershed protection, carbon sequestration) that are not priced in the market. By seizing land for conservation or ecological restoration, the government can preserve these public goods that would otherwise be degraded by private development. Below‑market compensation is sometimes justified on the basis that the social value of the land exceeds its market value, and that the owner should not be compensated for speculative value created by public environmental policies.
  • Mitigating Negative Externalities: Properties that generate pollution or other harms can be taken to eliminate the external costs they impose on surrounding communities. Compensation below market may reflect the fact that the property’s market value already incorporates these harmful uses.

2. Promoting Social Justice and Redistribution

  • Redistributive Economic Programs: Broad eminent domain can be used to implement land reform, affordable housing, or community development projects that directly reduce economic inequality. For example, seizing vacant or underused parcels to build low‑income housing can address housing shortages and segregation.
  • Correcting Historical Injustices: In some contexts, property acquisitions can be part of reparations or measures to rectify past dispossession of indigenous peoples or other marginalized groups. Compensation below market value may be seen as a modest contribution toward rectifying larger historical wrongs.

3. Overcoming Holdout Problems

  • Large‑scale infrastructure or social programs often require assembly of many contiguous parcels. Individual owners may hold out for exorbitant prices, stalling projects that deliver broad public benefits. Lowering compensation reduces the cost of acquisition, making such projects economically feasible and preventing opportunistic behavior.

4. Ensuring Efficient Land Use

  • Underused or abandoned properties (e.g., vacant lots, derelict factories) can be seized and repurposed for more socially beneficial uses. The government can argue that the market value of such land is low because its current use is inefficient, and that paying below market (e.g., the assessed value for tax purposes) is reasonable given the land’s limited productive contribution.

5. Fiscal Sustainability

  • Funding large public projects often strains government budgets. Allowing compensation below market value lowers the immediate fiscal outlay, freeing resources for other priorities or enabling a greater number of projects to be undertaken simultaneously.

6. Facilitating Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation

  • Protecting wetlands for flood control, creating green belts, or installing renewable energy infrastructure (e.g., solar farms, wind turbines) may require land that is currently in private hands. The urgency of climate action is used to justify more aggressive use of eminent domain with reduced compensation.

7. Encouraging Dynamic Efficiency

  • The threat of eminent domain can discourage landowners from engaging in rent‑seeking behavior, such as holding land idle in anticipation of future public projects that would inflate its value. A policy that limits compensation to something less than full market value can reduce these speculative gains.

Supposed Benefits of the Policy

  • More Ambitious Public Projects: Governments could tackle larger, more transformative initiatives (e.g., comprehensive coastal resilience plans, regional affordable housing programs) without being constrained by exorbitant acquisition costs.
  • Faster Implementation: Reduced negotiation times and lower risk of legal challenges over compensation could accelerate project timelines.
  • Greater Social Welfare Gains: By transferring property to uses with higher social value (e.g., parks, schools, clinics), the overall well‑being of the community can increase, even if individual owners receive less than market value.
  • Reduced Inequality: Land redistribution and the provision of public goods in underserved areas can help narrow the wealth gap and improve life outcomes for disadvantaged populations.
  • Environmental Stewardship: Preserving natural habitats and promoting sustainable land uses can protect biodiversity, improve public health, and contribute to long‑term ecological stability.

Philosophical and Legal Justifications (as Cited by Proponents)

  • The Social Obligation of Property: Some theories argue that property rights carry an inherent social responsibility; owners should not be allowed to use their property in ways that harm the community, and the community has a right to repurpose property for the common good.
  • The “Public Trust” Doctrine: In environmental law, certain natural resources are considered held in trust for the public. Expanding eminent domain can be seen as an extension of this principle to land that serves crucial ecological functions.
  • Lockean Proviso: John Locke’s labor theory of property includes the condition that there must be “enough and as good left in common” for others. When property accumulation leads to scarcity or environmental degradation, eminent domain can be used to restore balance.
  • Civic Republicanism: This perspective emphasizes that the state may prioritize civic virtue and the common interest over individual property claims, especially when the latter obstruct collective decision‑making.

Conclusion

Proponents of broadening eminent domain authority maintain that the policy is essential for tackling pressing social and environmental challenges. They argue that allowing compensation below market value is justified by the disproportionate benefits to society, the need to curb speculation, and the imperative to achieve more equitable and sustainable outcomes. While such proposals are often contentious due to concerns about property rights and fairness, the perceived benefits include more efficient land use, accelerated public projects, and a stronger capacity to address inequality and climate change.

Title: Reimagining Eminent Domain for the Public Good

Introduction
Eminent domain—the power of governments to seize private property for public use—has traditionally been justified by the necessity of critical infrastructure projects, such as roads, bridges, and public buildings. This concept, enshrined in many legal systems around the world, recognizes that at times, an individual’s property rights must yield to the greater social welfare. In recent years, however, pressing challenges like income inequality, housing shortages, environmental degradation, and uneven economic development reveal that the narrow traditional focus of eminent domain is insufficient. By radically expanding eminent domain powers to allow broader property seizures, including for economic redistribution and environmental initiatives, governments can levy this tool to achieve urgent social and economic goals. Moreover, providing minimal or below-market compensation to property owners can ensure that limited public funds are channeled toward initiatives that maximize societal benefits.

  1. Addressing Severe Housing Shortages and Economic Inequality
    The gap between the wealthy and the underprivileged has intensified, leading to widespread housing crises in urban centers. Tight real estate markets drive up prices, excluding many from access to affordable homes. Expanded eminent domain powers would give local and national governments more flexibility to appropriate properties sitting vacant, repurpose underutilized buildings, and construct social housing or community centers.
    • Providing affordable housing: When large tracts of land held by speculators are confiscated with minimal compensation, the savings from the depressed compensation cost can be redirected into construction and maintenance of public housing.
    • Redistributing wealth: Government seizure of large estates, luxury condominiums, or excessively spacious properties for reallocation can also help address wealth disparities. Authorities could strategically transform these developments into multi-unit dwellings, community centers, or small-business hubs, creating opportunities and spaces that economically marginalized groups previously lacked.
    • Diminishing speculative practices: By signaling that vacant and unused properties may be seized, governments discourage speculative investment, thereby stabilizing real estate prices and promoting responsible land use.

  2. Bolstering Environmental and Sustainability Initiatives
    Climate change and environmental degradation present urgent global crises that demand swift, large-scale responses from public authorities. Expanded eminent domain powers allow governments to acquire land for conservation, reforestation, or renewable energy projects without protracted legal battles or excessive financial outlay.
    • Preserving vital ecosystems: Sensitive areas such as wetlands, forests, and coastal regions can be permanently protected through seizure, ensuring that short-term commercial interests do not trump long-term ecological needs.
    • Advancing renewable energy projects: Solar farms, wind farms, and other environmentally beneficial installations often require large tracts of land, which can be difficult to assemble through normal market negotiations. Local communities will gain new energy sources and job opportunities if land acquisition is simplified.
    • Expanding greener infrastructure: Parks, bike paths, and nature reserves foster cleaner air, mitigate climate risks, and increase quality of life. Rapid access to these spaces via eminent domain can transform urban centers plagued by pollution and overcrowding.

  3. Streamlining State and Local Development Plans
    The conventional use of eminent domain is fraught with delays and legal disputes over compensation, especially when governments must pay market—or above-market—rates. Easing the compensation requirement yields quick, decisive action.
    • Faster project timelines: State and local agencies can initiate and complete crucial infrastructure projects at a fraction of the usual cost, saving public finances for further investment in social services and technology.
    • Reducing corruption and backroom deals: When property purchases and compensation amounts are subject to negotiation, opportunities abound for misuse of power and favoritism. A clear framework for minimal compensation treats all property owners equally, reducing the space for influence-peddling.
    • Enabling cohesive urban planning: Urban sprawl and fragmented land ownership create inefficient, disjointed cityscapes. Municipalities can better coordinate public transit, utilities, and zoning reforms by seizing strategically important properties rather than navigating a patchwork of protracted individual sales.

  4. Enhancing Community Resilience in Times of Crisis
    From natural disasters to economic downturns, governments often need to act swiftly in the face of emergencies. Expanded eminent domain, with limited compensation, equips them to respond effectively.
    • Deploying immediate relief efforts: In the wake of hurricanes, floods, or wildfires, the ability to obtain land quickly to set up relief camps, distribute supplies, or relocate populations is crucial.
    • Reconfiguring disaster-prone areas: Some regions face recurring hazards—coastal areas threatened by rising sea levels or earthquake-prone zones. Swift property seizure and relocation measures can save lives and reduce long-term societal costs.
    • Mitigating public health crises: When pandemics strike, authorities may need to convert land or properties into medical facilities urgently. Eminent domain expansions allow such conversions to happen rapidly without drawn-out compensation disputes.

  5. Establishing a More Equitable Society
    High compensation for private property often results in mounting public debt while benefiting only a small cadre of wealthier property owners. By minimizing or fixing compensation below market rates, governments can stretch public resources further.
    • Funding essential public services: Freed-up funds could be directed to schools, healthcare, and public infrastructure. This approach addresses fundamental social inequities by increasing the scope of services for all citizens.
    • Lowering the tax burden on average citizens: If authorities overpay for property, taxpayers shoulder the burden, often suffering regressive impacts.     • Promoting collective welfare: The premise of property rights generally rests on individual benefits, but radical expansion of eminent domain grounds property rights in collective responsibility. Critics may argue that these measures infringe on fundamental property rights or that minimal compensation is tantamount to legalized theft. Radical expansion of eminent domain powers, including the seizure of private property for social and economic goals beyond conventional infrastructure, represents a bold but necessary path. Housing crises, income inequality, environmental emergencies, and the need for cohesive urban planning demand forceful state intervention. Minimal or below-market compensation ensures that public funds are not unduly burdened while incentivizing efficient land use. Although this approach challenges traditional conceptions of property rights, it reaffirms a fundamental democratic principle: the well-being of the majority must come before the conveniences of the few. By proceeding thoughtfully yet decisively, governments can harness eminent domain to create more equitable, resilient, and sustainable societies for current and future generations.

The Case for Radically Expanding Eminent Domain: Reclaiming Public Power Over Private Land

A Persuasive Essay

Introduction

The Fifth Amendment's Takings Clause — "nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation" — has long been treated as a near-sacred boundary between government authority and individual rights. Yet this reverence for the status quo masks an uncomfortable truth: the current framework of eminent domain, narrowly constrained and generously compensating those who often least need generosity, has become a structural barrier to addressing the most pressing crises of our time. Climate catastrophe, staggering wealth inequality, housing scarcity, and ecological collapse all demand a fundamental reimagining of the relationship between private property and public need. The time has come to radically expand eminent domain powers — broadening the definition of "public use" to encompass economic redistribution and environmental stewardship while rethinking compensation frameworks that currently reward entrenched wealth at the expense of collective survival.

This is not a modest proposal for tinkering at the margins. It is an argument that the philosophical, legal, economic, and moral foundations of expansive eminent domain are far stronger than our political culture has been willing to acknowledge, and that the costs of inaction vastly exceed the costs of bold reform.

I. The Philosophical Foundations: Property as Social Convention

The case for expanded eminent domain begins with a foundational truth that defenders of strong property rights routinely obscure: private property is not a natural right but a social institution, created, maintained, and enforced by collective action through the state.

John Locke, often invoked as the patron saint of property rights, himself recognized limits. His labor theory of ownership included the crucial "Lockean proviso" — that appropriation is legitimate only when "enough and as good" is left for others. In a world of finite land, extreme concentration, and ecological limits, this proviso has been catastrophically violated. When three American families own more wealth than the bottom half of the population combined, when corporations hold millions of acres idle or ecologically degraded while communities lack housing and arable land, the Lockean justification for existing property distributions collapses under its own logic.

Thomas Jefferson understood this instinctively. "The earth belongs in usufruct to the living," he wrote to James Madison in 1789, arguing that no generation has the right to bind future generations to property arrangements that no longer serve them. Jeremy Bentham was even more direct: property is "entirely the work of law," and its justification lies solely in its utility to society. When existing property arrangements produce mass suffering, environmental destruction, and social instability, the utilitarian case for restructuring them is overwhelming.

Even conservative political philosophy provides resources here. The common-law tradition has always recognized that property rights are a "bundle of sticks" — a collection of use rights, access rights, and transfer rights that can be reconfigured by the sovereign authority that created them. Zoning laws, environmental regulations, building codes, and taxation all represent exercises of this principle that are thoroughly accepted in mainstream jurisprudence. Expanding eminent domain is not a departure from this tradition but its logical extension to meet contemporary challenges.

The philosophical case is straightforward: if property rights are justified by their social utility, and if current property arrangements are producing catastrophic social disutility, then society has not merely the right but the obligation to restructure those arrangements through its most direct available tool.

II. Legal Precedent: The Ground Is Already Prepared

Those who would characterize expanded eminent domain as radical legal innovation are either unfamiliar with or deliberately obscuring the existing trajectory of American jurisprudence.

The Supreme Court's 2005 decision in Kelo v. City of New London already established that "public use" encompasses "public purpose" — including economic development that benefits private parties. Writing for the majority, Justice Stevens affirmed that legislatures deserve broad deference in determining what constitutes public benefit: "Promoting economic development is a traditional and long-accepted function of government." The Court explicitly rejected a narrow reading that would limit takings to roads, bridges, and government buildings.

Kelo built on decades of precedent. In Berman v. Parker (1954), the Court upheld the condemnation of non-blighted property within a blighted area for redevelopment, declaring that "the concept of the public welfare is broad and inclusive." In Hawaii Housing Authority v. Midkiff (1984), the Court approved a statutory scheme that took land from large landowners and redistributed it to tenants — an explicitly redistributive purpose — finding that breaking up a land oligopoly served a legitimate public purpose.

Midkiff is particularly instructive. Hawaii's concentrated land ownership was producing housing unaffordability and economic distortion. The Court held unanimously that redistributing property to correct market failures and reduce inequality fell squarely within the government's eminent domain authority. Justice O'Connor — later a Kelo dissenter — wrote: "The mere fact that property taken outright by the State is transferred in the first instance to private beneficiaries does not condemn that taking as having only a private purpose."

The legal infrastructure for expansive eminent domain already exists. What is needed is the political will to build upon it — to recognize that if economic development and oligopoly-breaking constitute valid public purposes, then so too must climate adaptation, ecological restoration, wealth redistribution, and housing justice.

International law provides additional support. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights establishes rights to adequate housing, food, and a clean environment. When private property arrangements obstruct the realization of these rights, international human rights frameworks support state intervention to restructure them. Many nations — from South Africa's post-apartheid land reform provisions to Germany's constitutional subordination of property to social obligation (Article 14 of the Basic Law: "Property entails obligations. Its use shall also serve the public good") — demonstrate that robust democracies can and do subordinate property rights to social imperatives.

III. The Environmental Imperative: Survival Demands Seizure

Climate change presents the most urgent case for expanded eminent domain. The scientific consensus is unambiguous: avoiding civilizational catastrophe requires rapid, transformative action on a scale incompatible with voluntary market transactions and the glacial pace of willing-seller negotiations.

Consider the concrete challenges. Transitioning to renewable energy requires massive deployment of solar arrays, wind farms, transmission lines, and energy storage facilities. Current eminent domain frameworks — designed for linear infrastructure like highways and pipelines — are inadequate for the distributed, landscape-scale transformation required. Utility-scale solar requires approximately five acres per megawatt; achieving even modest decarbonization targets demands millions of acres. Negotiating individual transactions with thousands of landowners introduces delays measured in decades — time we do not have.

Coastal retreat presents an even starker case. Rising seas will render millions of properties uninhabitable within decades. Managed retreat — relocating communities away from doomed coastlines — is infinitely more humane and cost-effective than waiting for catastrophic flooding to accomplish the same displacement chaotically. But managed retreat requires the government to acquire vast swaths of coastal property, often over the objections of owners in denial about the physical realities confronting their land. Paying full market value for property that the ocean will claim regardless represents an unconscionable waste of public resources — resources desperately needed for building resilient communities inland.

Ecological restoration demands similar authority. Reconnecting fragmented wildlife corridors, restoring wetlands that provide flood protection and carbon sequestration, and reforesting degraded landscapes all require assembling contiguous parcels from unwilling sellers. The holdout problem — where individual owners demand extortionate prices knowing their parcel is essential to a larger project — makes voluntary assembly economically and practically impossible at the necessary scale.

Below-market compensation in environmental takings is not merely defensible but ethically required. Much of the "value" of environmentally sensitive land reflects speculative development potential that responsible regulation should never have permitted. Compensating owners for the full speculative value of wetlands they would have drained, forests they would have clearcut, or coastlines they would have armored with seawalls rewards the very behavior that created the environmental crisis. A compensation framework reflecting the land's ecologically appropriate use — rather than its most profitable destructive use — aligns private incentives with collective survival.

Moreover, much private land value derives not from owner investment but from public goods: government-built roads, publicly funded schools, community-created amenities, and the stability provided by the legal system itself. Henry George recognized in the 19th century that land values are overwhelmingly created by community action, not individual effort. Requiring the public to pay full market value to reclaim value it largely created represents a perverse subsidy to passive wealth.

IV. Economic Redistribution: Breaking the Property Trap

Wealth inequality in the United States has reached levels that threaten democratic governance, social stability, and economic efficiency. Property — particularly real property — is the primary mechanism through which inequality reproduces itself across generations. Expanding eminent domain to serve redistributive purposes directly addresses the structural roots of this crisis.

The numbers are stark. The top 10% of Americans own approximately 70% of the nation's wealth, with real estate constituting a massive share. This concentration is not the product of superior effort or talent but of compounding historical advantages — including, in the American context, centuries of racialized land theft, exclusionary zoning, discriminatory lending, and regressive tax policy. The current distribution of property reflects not market meritocracy but accumulated injustice.

Redistributive eminent domain could take multiple forms. Vacant and underutilized urban land held by speculators could be seized and developed as affordable housing, community land trusts, or cooperative enterprises. Agricultural land concentrated in the hands of corporate agribusinesses could be redistributed to small farmers, beginning farmers, and historically dispossessed communities. Excessive corporate land holdings could be broken up, as Hawaii successfully did under the scheme upheld in Midkiff.

The economic efficiency arguments are powerful. Land hoarding and speculation impose enormous deadweight losses on the economy. Vacant lots in cities with housing crises, productive farmland held fallow for speculative appreciation, and commercial properties deliberately kept empty to maintain artificial scarcity all represent market failures that eminent domain can correct. Redistributing these resources to productive users generates economic activity, tax revenue, and social value that dwarfs the losses to existing owners.

Below-market compensation in redistributive contexts is justified by several considerations. First, much concentrated property ownership traces to historical injustices — land theft from Indigenous peoples, exploitation of enslaved labor, discriminatory exclusion of minorities from property markets — for which the current "owners" never provided just compensation to those originally dispossessed. Requiring the public to pay full market value to remedy these injustices forces victims to purchase their own restitution. Second, speculative land value represents a socially created surplus that the owner did nothing to earn; capturing this surplus for public benefit is a matter of basic fairness. Third, progressive compensation — paying small holders full value while offering large holders decreasing marginal compensation — would target redistribution precisely where it is needed while protecting ordinary homeowners.

Critics will invoke the specter of Soviet collectivization or Venezuelan expropriation. This is intellectually dishonest. Expanding eminent domain within a democratic legal framework, subject to legislative authorization and judicial review, bears no resemblance to authoritarian seizure. Democratic societies routinely redistribute property through taxation, regulation, and spending; eminent domain is simply a more direct and transparent mechanism for accomplishing the same ends. The question is not whether the state may redistribute — it manifestly does, constantly — but whether it may do so efficiently and honestly.

V. The Compensation Question: Rethinking "Just"

The most provocative element of this proposal — below-market compensation — deserves careful defense, because it is in many ways the most important.

"Just compensation" in current jurisprudence is defined as fair market value — the price a willing buyer would pay a willing seller in an arm's-length transaction. This standard is treated as self-evidently fair, but it is in fact deeply problematic.

Market value reflects existing distributions of wealth, power, and legal privilege. When those distributions are themselves unjust — as the historical record overwhelmingly demonstrates — market value merely crystallizes injustice into a price tag. Paying "fair market value" for land stolen from Indigenous nations launders centuries of dispossession through the cleansing mechanism of market pricing. Paying full market value for properties whose value derives from exclusionary zoning that kept minorities out rewards discrimination. The market is not a neutral arbiter of value; it is an institution that reflects and amplifies existing power relations.

Furthermore, market value includes speculative components that represent no genuine social contribution. When a vacant urban lot is valued at millions of dollars because of anticipated future development, that value reflects community growth, public infrastructure investment, and zoning decisions — not owner effort. Requiring the public to pay for the value it created is circular and wasteful.

A reformed compensation framework might operate on several principles. Owner-occupied primary residences could receive full market value plus relocation assistance, protecting the genuine shelter interests and emotional attachments of ordinary families. Small businesses could receive full compensation for documented losses and transition support. But large commercial holdings, speculative land banks, and corporate agricultural operations would receive compensation based on the land's current productive use value — excluding speculative premiums — or its assessed tax value, whichever is lower. This last provision introduces an elegant accountability mechanism: owners who have systematically underreported property values to minimize tax obligations would receive compensation based on their own declared valuations.

This tiered approach is not unprecedented. Tax policy already treats different categories of property and income differently. Progressive taxation embodies the principle that the marginal social value of a dollar decreases as wealth increases. The same principle justifies progressive compensation: taking a family's home is categorically different from taking a corporation's land bank, and compensation should reflect this moral reality.

VI. Addressing Objections

"This would destroy investment incentives." This objection assumes that the threat of seizure would deter productive use of land. But the opposite is true: the threat of seizure for underutilization would incentivize productive use. Owners who develop their land, maintain it responsibly, and put it to socially valuable purposes would face minimal risk. Speculators, hoarders, and those whose land use generates negative externalities would face the greatest exposure — which is precisely the incentive structure a rational policy should create.

"The slippery slope to tyranny." Democratic oversight provides the essential safeguard. Expanded eminent domain would operate through legislative authorization, administrative process, and judicial review — the same institutional framework that governs existing takings. The risk of abuse is real but manageable through procedural protections: public hearings, impact assessments, democratic accountability at the ballot box, and independent judicial review of both the taking's purpose and the adequacy of compensation. Every expansion of government power carries risks; the question is whether those risks outweigh the certain harms of inaction.

"Property rights are the foundation of liberty." This claim confuses cause and effect. Property rights are instrumentally valuable because they promote autonomy, security, and productive activity. When property concentration becomes so extreme that it undermines these values for the majority — when millions cannot afford shelter while speculators hold land vacant, when corporate land monopolies destroy rural communities, when fossil fuel interests block the energy transition necessary for human survival — then the "liberty" protected by property rights has become the liberty of the few to endanger the many. Genuine liberty requires a material foundation accessible to all, not paper rights protecting concentrated wealth.

"Markets are more efficient than government allocation." Markets are efficient at maximizing returns to capital. They are structurally incapable of valuing public goods, long-term ecological sustainability, social equity, or intergenerational justice. The climate crisis is itself the most spectacular market failure in human history — the product of markets that systematically externalized environmental costs onto the public and future generations. Invoking market efficiency to oppose the corrective measures necessitated by market failure is not an argument; it is a tautology.

VII. Historical Precedent and Comparative Success

History demonstrates that aggressive property redistribution, when democratically enacted, can produce transformative social benefits.

The Homestead Acts of the 19th century — which redistributed vast tracts of (admittedly stolen Indigenous) land to individual settlers — created the American middle class. The New Deal's rural electrification and agricultural programs restructured property relations across the American countryside. Post-World War II land reforms in Japan, South Korea, and Taiwan — carried out under American guidance — broke up feudal landholding patterns and laid the foundation for the economic miracles that followed. In each case, concentrated land ownership was identified as a barrier to economic development and social stability, and redistribution produced broadly shared prosperity.

South Africa's post-apartheid constitution explicitly authorizes expropriation for land reform at below-market compensation, recognizing that requiring full market value for land acquired through racialized dispossession would make justice financially impossible. Scotland's Land Reform Act of 2003 granted communities the right to purchase rural land compulsorily, breaking up the vast estates that concentrated ownership among a tiny aristocratic class. Singapore's aggressive land acquisition program — which acquired vast private land holdings at below-market rates — enabled the public housing system that today houses 80% of the population in high-quality, affordable units.

These examples demonstrate that expanded eminent domain is not utopian fantasy but proven policy — effective precisely in proportion to its boldness.

VIII. A Moral Imperative

Ultimately, the case for expanded eminent domain rests on a moral proposition: when private property arrangements produce mass homelessness, ecological catastrophe, entrenched racial inequality, and existential threats to human civilization, the moral claims of property owners are subordinate to the claims of human survival and justice.

We do not permit property rights to shield owners from fire codes, health regulations, or civil rights laws. We recognize that ownership confers obligations as well as privileges. The argument advanced here simply extends this recognition to its logical conclusion: in a time of converging crises, the obligation of property to serve the common good must take precedence over the privilege of owners to maximize private returns.

The children who will inherit a destabilized climate did not consent to the property arrangements that produced it. The families priced out of housing markets by speculation and hoarding did not choose their dispossession. The communities of color whose ancestors were robbed of land and wealth did not agree to the intergenerational theft that defines their material circumstances. These voiceless constituencies — future generations, the displaced, the historically dispossessed — have claims that no market transaction can satisfy and no compensation formula can capture. Their interests can be vindicated only by a state willing to exercise its sovereign authority over the property arrangements that harm them.

Conclusion

The expansion of eminent domain proposed here is admittedly radical. It challenges deeply held assumptions about the sanctity of property and the limits of state power. But the crises we face — climate collapse, structural inequality, ecological destruction, housing scarcity — are themselves radical, and they demand responses commensurate with their scale.

The philosophical foundations of property rights support, rather than preclude, robust public authority over private land. The legal precedents are already in place, awaiting only political courage to build upon them. The economic arguments for redistributive efficiency and against speculative hoarding are compelling. The environmental imperative is existential. And the moral case — that human survival and social justice outweigh the entitlements of concentrated wealth — is, in the final analysis, unanswerable.

We need not apologize for asserting that society's claim to its own survival supersedes any individual's claim to speculative profit. The earth belongs to the living, and the living are running out of time.

By Chester Pemberton III, Staff Writer, The Quarterly Bulldozer

WASHINGTON — A growing coalition of property owners, constitutional scholars, and people who definitely read the entire Fifth Amendment and not just the part they liked gathered on the steps of the Capitol this week to protest proposed expansions of eminent domain authority. Their signs read "DON'T TREAD ON MY DEED" and "MY LAND, MY RULES," which is also, coincidentally, what several of them say about zoning laws they personally benefit from.

"This is tyranny," declared Hank Moorfield, a retired contractor who built his fortune on government highway contracts that were only possible because of — and I cannot stress this enough — eminent domain. "The government has no right to take someone's property just because thousands of people might benefit. What about MY feelings?"

When asked if he had supported the seizure of farmland to build the interstate exit that tripled his own property value in 1987, Moorfield said that was "completely different" and then pretended to receive a phone call.

THE FOUNDERS WOULD HAVE AGREED WITH ME SPECIFICALLY

The anti-eminent-domain movement has found unlikely intellectual leadership in Dr. Patricia Covington, a libertarian scholar at the Randolph Freedom Institute, which operates out of a building that was, per public records, a church until the city seized it in 1954 to build a municipal parking lot that was later sold to a private developer who converted it into — I'm not making this up — the Randolph Freedom Institute.

"The Founders were absolutely clear," Dr. Covington told me, adjusting her glasses with the gravity of someone about to say something the Founders were not absolutely clear about. "Private property is sacrosanct."

I asked her about the Takings Clause, which explicitly contemplates the government taking private property. She called it "a limitation, not a permission."

I asked her about the fact that the Constitution literally says "nor shall private property be taken for public use, without just compensation" — the word "taken" doing some rather heavy lifting there in favor of the government's ability to, you know, take things.

She asked me to leave.

THE LITTLE GUY (WHO OWNS FOUR PROPERTIES)

Perhaps no figure better represents the movement than Dave and Linda Hutchins of Scottsdale, Arizona, who have become folk heroes after refusing to sell their 2,400-square-foot ranch home to make way for a proposed light rail extension that would serve approximately 40,000 daily commuters.

"We're just regular people standing up to the machine," Dave told Fox News, standing in front of a home Zillow estimates at $780,000.

The Hutchinses have launched a GoFundMe that has raised $340,000, which they plan to use for legal fees and also, according to the fine print, "property improvements and related personal expenses." They have also sold merchandise. You can buy a t-shirt that says "THIS LAND IS MY LAND" for $35, which represents a rather aggressive interpretation of Woody Guthrie's intentions.

Their neighbors, who overwhelmingly support the light rail project because they spend three hours a day in traffic, have been characterized by the movement as "sheeple." Several of these sheeple are nurses.

A BRIEF HISTORY OF THINGS THAT WOULDN'T EXIST

In the interest of journalistic balance, I should note that critics of eminent domain expansion make many valid points about government overreach, corruption, and the disproportionate impact on communities of color and low-income residents — points that are considerably undermined when the loudest voices in the movement are wealthy suburbanites worried about a bike lane.

I should also note, for fun, a partial list of things that required eminent domain and would not exist without it:

  • The Interstate Highway System
  • Most airports
  • The Hoover Dam
  • Central Park
  • Virtually every railroad
  • The National Mall
  • Most public universities' campuses
  • Dave Hutchins' favorite Costco

When presented with this list, movement spokesperson Roger Kelling said, "Well, obviously THOSE were necessary." He then refused to articulate a principle that distinguished those cases from current proposals, instead pivoting to a tangent about Thomas Jefferson that contained two factual errors and one quote actually attributable to Thomas Paine.

THE DEVELOPER IN THE ROOM

It would be irresponsible not to mention that the movement's largest donor is Patriot Property Alliance, a 501(c)(4) funded almost entirely by commercial real estate developers who are — and again, I must stress the irony — not opposed to eminent domain when it benefits them. They are opposed to eminent domain for public housing, parks, and transit.

Their president, a man named Cliff Deakins whose company has received land through eminent domain proceedings six times in the past decade, told me with a straight face that his organization stands for "the little guy."

I laughed. He did not.

"We believe property rights are the foundation of liberty," said Deakins, from an office built on land the city of Tampa condemned and handed to his company in 2016 for a mixed-use development that was supposed to include affordable housing units and does not.

THE KELO CROWD

No article about eminent domain opposition would be complete without mentioning Kelo v. City of New London (2005), the Supreme Court case that has become the movement's Alamo. In Kelo, the Court ruled that economic development qualified as "public use," allowing the city to transfer seized land to private developers.

The decision was, to be fair, genuinely controversial. Many legal scholars across the political spectrum found it troubling. The backlash was enormous and bipartisan.

What the movement prefers not to mention is that they have used Kelo — a case about private development — to oppose virtually all eminent domain, including cases involving actual public infrastructure that even the most conservative justices would rubber-stamp while half asleep.

"Kelo changed everything," said protester Megan Ainsley, who was holding a sign depicting Justice Stevens as a vampire. When I asked her if she opposed the use of eminent domain to build her children's public school, she said, "That's a gotcha question."

It was, admittedly, a gotcha question. But it also had an answer, and she didn't have one.

CONCLUSION: A MODEST PROPOSAL

In closing, I want to be fair to the property rights movement. There are legitimate, serious concerns about eminent domain abuse. The history of "urban renewal" destroying Black neighborhoods is a genuine horror. The potential for corruption is real. Compensation is often inadequate. These are important conversations.

It's just hard to have them when the conversation is dominated by people whose actual position is "the government should be able to build things, just not near me, and also I would like to keep collecting the property value gains that resulted from the government building things near me previously."

Perhaps we could reach a compromise: the government agrees to stop using eminent domain entirely, and in exchange, everyone who has ever benefited from it gives back the proceeds. Dave Hutchins can start by returning that $780,000 home to the desert it was before the Bureau of Reclamation seized half of Arizona to build the canal system that supplies his water.

I'll wait.

Chester Pemberton III is a fictional columnist and does not own property because he is not real and also because, if he were, he could not afford it, which is arguably the whole problem.

Second, we must reform compensation standards. "Just compensation" has been interpreted to mean inflated market value that rewards speculation and punishes the public treasury. Compensation should be fair — but fair to both parties. It should reflect actual use value, not speculative future value. It should account for the public investments — roads, utilities, schools — that created that property value in the first place. The community helped build that value; the community deserves to share in it.

Third, we must streamline the acquisition process. Years of litigation benefit only lawyers while communities suffer. We need expedited review, rapid possession authority, and limits on frivolous challenges designed merely to extract higher payments.

Fourth, we must empower not just federal but state and local governments — and yes, even designated development authorities — to exercise these powers when they can demonstrate a compelling public benefit.

To the critics, I say this:

You will call this socialism. But every highway you drive on, every airport you fly from, every reservoir that delivers your water was built on land acquired through eminent domain. The entire American West was developed through government land policy that prioritized collective development over individual claims.

You will say this invites abuse. Then let us build in safeguards — transparency requirements, community input processes, independent review boards, anti-corruption measures. The answer to potential abuse is accountability, not paralysis.

You will say this violates fundamental rights. But rights exist in relationship to one another. Your right to hold property does not supersede my community's right to survive, to thrive, to adapt to climate change, to house its people, to build its future.

The great projects of American civilization — the transcontinental railroad, the interstate highway system, the Tennessee Valley Authority, the national parks — all required the assertion of public power over private claims. Every single one was opposed by property interests who said the government was overreaching. And every single one transformed this nation for the better.

We stand at a similar crossroads today.

Climate change demands that we relocate communities, restore wetlands, build seawalls, and construct renewable energy at a scale never before attempted. The housing crisis demands that we assemble land in our most productive cities for the homes our people desperately need. I say we choose the common good. I say we choose the future. I say we build.
